articles.title: Covering the Big Tigers in China: Patronage Ties and Political Signaling within Elite Circles
articles.abstract: Official media in authoritarian regimes typically supports pro-government narratives, yet it also reports on high-ranking officials after corruption investigations into them, despite risking public criticism and offering little new information to central leaders. Why does this occur? I argue that such reporting functions as intra-elite signaling. The central media’s selective focus on certain disgraced officials helps autocrats signal power consolidation, while local media imitation allows local elites to display loyalty. Using an original dataset of news reports on high-ranking officials investigated during China’s anti-corruption campaign (2012–2017), I find that central media disproportionately targeted “big tigers” linked to the top leader’s political rivals. Local media largely mirrored this pattern, highlighting the strategic role of official media in managing relations between autocrats and other elites.

articles.title: Group Identity and Belief Formation: A Microfoundation of Political Polarization
articles.authors: Kevin Bauer, Yan Chen, Florian Hett, Michael Kosfeld
articles.abstract: To evaluate the impact of group identity on belief formation, we conducted online experiments before and after the 2020 US presidential election. We elicit participants’ beliefs about future unemployment statistics and health system rankings and provide relevant news summaries. We find that people pay money to avoid information from political outgroups and attribute lower weight to this information when updating beliefs. An intervention which unlabels information sources decreases outgroup information avoidance by 50%, with a significant impact on only groupish participants. A debiasing intervention equalizing instrumental values of information sources reduces only universalists’ WTP for a private signal. The interventions have little effect on information processing. The evidence is consistent with a source-utility channel contributing to polarization.

articles.title: Demographic transition and the rise of wealth inequality
articles.authors: Krzysztof Makarski, Joanna Tyrowicz, Piotr Żoch
articles.abstract: We analyse the contribution of rising longevity to the increase in wealth inequality in the U.S. over the past seventy years. To do so, we construct an overlapping generations (OLG) model with multiple sources of inequality, carefully calibrated to the data. Our key finding is that improvements in old-age longevity have a substantial impact on wealth inequality, accounting for approximately half the effect of income inequality, which has been the focus of much of the existing literature. In contrast, the impact of tax changes is relatively minor. The contribution of rising longevity is expected to continue driving wealth inequality upward in the coming decades.

articles.title: Political Polarization and Counter-attitudinal Information Consumption and Internalization
articles.abstract: Political polarization can undermine democratic governance by weakening electoral accountability through biases in voter information consumption and processing. A growing literature, primarily from high-income countries, has identified promising interventions to reduce negative affect toward out-partisans, though evidence regarding their downstream effects remains mixed. We evaluate whether these depolarizing interventions and an open-mindedness nudge that increases awareness of information-processing biases stemming from emotions or partisanship promote counter-attitudinal information consumption and internalization in a survey of nearly 2,500 participants from a nationally representative panel in Mexico, a heavily polarized context. Videos designed to correct misperceptions about out-partisans improved trust in opposition media, while those designed to foster empathy or emphasize shared identities reduced partisan polarization. Although none of the videos affected immediate counter-attitudinal news consumption, exposure to either the corrective video or the open-mindedness nudge led to greater partisan attitudinal updating when participants were exposed to a counter-attitudinal news article. This effect is due to reduced partisan perceptions of the article rather than increased factual retention of its information. These findings provide insights into the potential and limitations of scalable interventions to improve citizens’ ability to consume and process politically relevant information across partisan lines.

articles.title: A Comment on “The Heterogeneous Tax Pass-Through Under Different Vertical Relationships” by Bajo-Buenestado and Borrella-Mas
articles.abstract: We revisit the heterogeneous tax pass-through analysis in Borrella-Mas (2022a) (B&B). We find that B&B’s estimating equation is misspecified, as it excludes a necessary lower-order interaction between vertical integration and the post-treatment period. Including this term reveals a significant structural price trend for vertically integrated firms in the post-reform period, whose origin is uncertain. A spatial placebo test confirms that this structural shift is present even in never-treated provinces, indicating that it is not a local, province-level pass-through of the regional tax. Without this control, the original specification may conflate this shift with the tax effect. Once the interaction is included, the differential pass-through estimate becomes null for diesel, while for gasoline a significant effect persists—albeit at a reduced magnitude—supporting B&B’s central claim that market structure matters for tax pass-through. These findings highlight the importance of explicitly modelling group-specific time trends when estimating heterogeneous treatment effects in difference-in-differences designs.

articles.title: Remote work and effort provision in teams
articles.authors: E Glenn Dutcher, Krista J Saral
articles.abstract: Remote work policies remain controversial partly because of productivity concerns, which are potentially exacerbated in team settings. Using experiments, we isolate how location-based beliefs of teammate effort affect the own-effort choices of participants assigned to work with remote and office-based teammates. Participants perform a real effort task and can contribute this effort to an individual account, paying a piece rate wage, or to a team account using a minimum-effort payment scheme. We find that remote workers do not complete fewer tasks than their office-based counterparts. Yet, teams suffer from lower effort due to workers responding to beliefs that remote teammates contribute less effort to the team. In a follow-up treatment, we demonstrate that these location-based beliefs remain salient even under a revenue-sharing team payment scheme where beliefs of free-riding may have dominated. Finally, we provide unique evidence that the COVID-19 pandemic may have shifted beliefs to be more pessimistic about the effort of remote workers but did not alter the actual effort.

articles.title: Rethinking Mobile Ethnography: Spatial and Social Experiences of Older Migrants
articles.authors: Tuğçe Tezel, Basak Bilecen, Nardi Steverink
articles.abstract: Europe's ageing population includes a growing number of older migrants whose experiences of ageing in place require methods that capture mobility, place, and social participation. Mobile ethnography, particularly walking/go‐along interviews, offers valuable opportunities to examine how older migrants engage with everyday environments. Yet existing mobile research with older migrants has often focused on participants able to take part in walking interviews, leaving less attention to how mobile ethnography can be applied with migrants in advanced age and with different mobility conditions. Drawing on fieldwork with migrants from Turkey in Germany, nearly all aged 70 and above, this paper develops a more flexible understanding of mobility within mobile ethnography. It shows how engagement with place can be explored through walking, but also through familiar community settings, shorter movements, narrated routes, remembered places, supported mobility, and repeated everyday routines. The paper offers a more inclusive methodological approach for research with ageing migrant populations.

articles.title: A Gamified Strategy to Resist Migration Disinformation in Adolescents
articles.abstract: Migration‐related disinformation has become increasingly prominent in online environments, particularly in the context of war‐related migration and polarized public discourse. Adolescents may be especially vulnerable to manipulative online narratives due to ongoing cognitive and social development. This study examined whether the gamified inoculation intervention Bad News could strengthen adolescents' resistance to migration‐related disinformation. A quasi‐experimental pre–post design was conducted among Czech secondary school students aged 16–18 ( N = 235). Participants evaluated simulated social media posts before and after gameplay using measures of perceived credibility and confidence. Truth discernment was defined as the difference between credibility ratings of accurate and misleading content. Results showed reduced perceived credibility of disinformation, increased confidence in evaluation, and improved truth discernment following gameplay. Overall belief remained unchanged, suggesting improved discrimination rather than generalized scepticism. The findings support the educational potential of gamified inoculation approaches for strengthening adolescents' resilience to migration‐related disinformation.

articles.title: La Muerte del Coyote: Human Smuggling in the Age of Asylum
articles.authors: Jeremy Slack, Emilio Alberto López Reyes
articles.abstract: Over the last decade, the prominence of asylum or asylum‐adjacent migration has overtaken undocumented migration, where many people are seeking to hand themselves into authorities rather than avoid detection. This has dramatically altered services offered by human smugglers. This article explores how smugglers adapted to current migration processes at the border and what strategies have been employed to continue to be profitable. By building on the ‘migration industry’ framework, we explore how illegal enterprises evolve in response to changes in migration policy in ways that both facilitate migration but also hinder migration and seek rents. This article expands on the concept of ‘bastard’ industries, helping understand how and why smuggling has developed an interconnected network of kidnapping and extortion. We argue that these changes expose some fundamental aspects of smuggling rather than representing an aberration of the smuggling industry.

articles.title: Playing Hard to Get: Strategic Signaling in Aid Bargaining
articles.abstract: Foreign aid is a political exchange between a donor and a target. Existing literature focuses primarily on the strategic actions of donors, but less is known about how targets advance their interests. This article explores the role of aid-receiving states as strategic actors who can extract concessions from donors. I model the aid exchange using a costly signaling model in which targets send a (potentially misleading) signal of their policy preferences before the donor makes an aid offer. In equilibrium, when the cost of sending a misleading signal is sufficiently low, targets who are aligned with a donor on policy sometimes lie about their alignment, which yields them aid that they would not have received otherwise. Empirically, I show that strategic nonresponse in the UN General Assembly—a low-cost signal of nonalignment—is correlated with higher future aid inflows.

articles.title: Beyond “non-significant” results: Why and how to test for practical equivalence
articles.authors: Jakub Tomek, Aaron Caldwell, David A. Eisner
articles.abstract: Reporting comparisons with P ≥ 0.05 as showing “no effect” or “no difference” remains one of the most widespread and problematic misinterpretations in the scientific literature. A statistically nonsignificant result shows only that the data do not provide strong evidence for a difference. This distinction matters because such findings can arise for two very different reasons: Either there is no meaningful difference, or a meaningful difference is present but cannot be detected reliably because of limited sample size or high variability. We highlight equivalence testing as a practical framework for distinguishing between these possibilities. Using the two one-sided tests (TOST) approach, investigators can formally test whether effects large enough to be scientifically, clinically, or practically meaningful can be ruled out. We explain the logic of TOST, show how it distinguishes practical equivalence from inconclusive evidence, and illustrate its use in paired and unpaired comparisons. To support broader adoption, we also introduce a freely available online calculator that enables researchers to perform common equivalence tests without coding.

articles.title: Value misalignments in X’s feed algorithm is a reflection of value tensions in engagement
articles.authors: Ziv Epstein, Farnaz Jahanbakhsh, Tiziano Piccardi, Axel Peytavin, Isabel Gallegos, Shardul Sapkota, Dora Zhao, Johan Ugander, Michael S. Bernstein
articles.abstract: Social media feed algorithms rank content that is purported to be preferred by users, but the engagement behaviors that drive these algorithms are (at best) indirect proxies for users’ explicitly self-stated values. Are the resulting feeds value aligned, and if not, why? We investigate this question by annotating the basic human values expressed in participants’ X (Twitter) feeds (N = 715 US users), analyzing the relationship between the posts’ value expressions and the posts’ amplification in the ranked “For You” Page feed, and then comparing the amplified values to users’ own values. We observe that the inventory of posts from followed accounts reflects users’ self-stated values—but that there is an overall negative correlation (misalignment) between users’ explicit values and the value expressions the algorithm is more likely to amplify. We turn to engagement behavior to understand this misalignment and observe that users’ engagement behaviors can be misaligned with their stated values—likely causing the algorithm to learn and reflect these misaligned values. We also detect partisan differences consistent with this theory: While the algorithm amplifies values negatively correlated with both Democrats’ and Republicans’ self-stated values, they are more misaligned for Democrats. And in fact replying, a heavily weighted form of engagement, is associated with values that are less aligned for both Democrats’ and Republicans’ self-stated values, and is even more misaligned for Democrats. Taken together, these findings offer a glimpse into the tensions between the values that people hold and those that provoke reactions, and how these value tensions can produce misaligned outcomes.

articles.title: The effectiveness of green place-based industrial policy: Evidence from the Inflation Reduction Act
articles.authors: Joep Keuzenkamp, Jacopo Mazza, Bob Rijkers, Katherine Stapleton
articles.abstract: Governments across the globe are turning to place-based industrial policies to make the green transition more equitable and politically palatable. The United States’ Inflation Reduction Act exemplifies this approach through its “Energy Community” provisions, which offer additional tax incentives for clean energy projects in regions reliant on fossil fuels. We use spatially granular data on renewable energy investment, employment, and voting, and document that these incentives substantially increased local solar investment, but we do not find significant impacts on wind investment, job creation, or political preferences. Estimated abatement costs are well below the social cost of carbon and lower than those of other major U.S. climate policies. The results suggest that place-based green industrial policies can effectively direct clean energy investment toward disadvantaged regions, but their capacity to generate broader local economic or political benefits may be limited.

However, since 1911 Robert Michels popularised the phrase of an “iron law of oligarchy” to argue how nominally democratic institutions, like worker cooperatives, often fall back into hierarchical patterns. I claim that this criticism against workplace democracy is based on a misreading of Michels’ philosophy and a misrepresentation of today’s empirical research on cooperative management. Both present worker cooperatives as hybrid institutions torn between oligarchic and democratic pulls. By counterbalancing tendencies towards a concentration of power at the top with countervailing institutions that help rank-and-file workers contest managerial decision-making, worker cooperatives can safeguard themselves against degeneration and the iron law of oligarchy. This proposal of instituting workplace democracy through constant anti-hierarchical conflict, I call “plebeian cooperativism.”

articles.title: Affirming democracy: Should we exaggerate support for democracy to save it?
articles.abstract: Democracies around the world have increasingly faced concerted efforts to dismantle democratic institutions. How should public speakers respond to such attempts at democratic backsliding? A widespread rhetorical strategy is to affirm democracy —that is, to publicly invoke the value of democracy and vigorously insist on the need to defend it. I argue that this practice gives rise to an underappreciated democratic dilemma. On one hand, distinctive features of the backsliding process seemingly require us to affirm democracy. Yet, on the other hand, this practice also poses serious dangers for democracy. For one, it risks accelerating democratic erosion. Moreover, efforts to limit this risk seemingly violate democratic requirements of truthfulness. So, both affirming democracy and failing to do so involve significant democratic pitfalls. The best way to navigate this dilemma, I contend, is not to forgo affirming democracy. Instead, it is to do so in a way that emphasises elites’ concrete attacks on democracy, while insisting that most people are strongly committed to democracy. While this approach may indeed involve some deception—insofar as it may knowingly overstate support for democracy—this is often all-things-considered justified.

articles.title: Popular tribunate or bourgeois populism? #saccageparis and social media’s radical-democratic paradox
articles.abstract: This article argues that the case of an idiosyncratic digital movement in Paris—#saccageparis—has much to contribute to recent debates around social media’s democratic potential. #saccageparis leaders paint themselves as contemporary tribunes of the plebs, a permanent counter-power representing the “small people” of Paris against the municipality. Based on ethnographic fieldwork, I examine in this article such claim. On the one hand, Twitter’s affordances enabled ordinary citizens to gain some of the attributes of a popular tribunate standing up to power while, on the other hand, the movement only gained this foothold because it was not itself popular. #saccageparis’s composition therefore contradicts its tactics, and the movement is best described as “bourgeois populism.” This case shows us how social media’s populist affordances can be exploited by elites and, as a result, offers precious insights for those interested in rescuing social media’s radical-democratic possibilities from elite capture.

articles.title: Agile Digital Transformation and the Rule of Law: Perks and Perils in a Belgian and a Dutch Public Sector Organization
articles.abstract: This paper examines the interplay between agile digital transformation and the rule of law within the public sector, focusing on case studies from a semi‐large municipal government in the Netherlands and a department of the Flemish regional government in Belgium. Drawing on expert interviews, the paper explores how agile methods, championed for flexibility, interact with existing administrative routines and affect rule of law principles that prioritize consistency. Theoretically, the paper builds on public administration scholarship concerning administrative routines and the rule of law. Empirically, the paper shows that agile methods align well with administrative routines that prioritize decentralized leadership and collaboration. Moreover, it shows that agile approaches can foster, rather than threaten, the rule of law: many legal uncertainties arise not from agile practices themselves but from existing complexities in laws and policies, highlighting a need for stronger technical precision in lawmaking and administrative awareness in digital implementation.

articles.title: From Social Equity Budgeting to Revenue Equity: Minority Leadership and Local Governments' Exploitative Revenues
articles.authors: Tingzhong Huang, Rui Wang, Can Chen, Herong Gao
articles.abstract: Social equity budgeting has gained increasing attention, yet research has largely focused on expenditures while neglecting revenue equity. This study contributes to the literature by examining the relationships between minority population size and local governments' reliance on exploitative revenues, and whether minority political representation moderates this relationship. Drawing on racial threat and political representation theories, we analyze data from 66 Florida counties between 2011 and 2019. Results show that counties with larger minority populations rely more heavily on exploitative revenues, but this relationship diminishes when minority political representation increases. These findings highlight how minority leadership could moderate fiscal practices that disproportionately burden minority communities. More broadly, this study advances the framework of social equity budgeting by shifting the focus from expenditure allocation to revenue generation.

articles.title: Organizational Capacity to Implement Social Equity in Emergency Management: A Local Government Perspective
articles.authors: Jason D. Rivera, Claire Connolly Knox, Clinton McNair, Joseph T. Ripberger
articles.abstract: The emergency management profession and discipline is increasingly embracing social equity as a core value, yet limited attention has been paid to whether local emergency management organizations possess the capacity to implement equity‐focused practices. Drawing on the Capacity Building Framework, this exploratory study analyzes data from a national panel survey of US emergency managers to examine the organizational capacity to advance social equity through the lens of adaptive capacity. The findings reveal that while political, technical, financial, and managerial capacities matter, financial capacity is the most critical constraint. Respondents prioritized additional funding for personnel, community outreach and education, and the development of accessible public resources. The results highlight how resource scarcity shapes the pursuit of equity at the local level and underscores the need to align equity goals with investments in organizational capacity. This study contributes insight into the practical challenges emergency managers face in translating equity commitments into action.

articles.title: Under Pressure: Analyzing LEO Turnover in America's Swing and Pivot Counties for 2016, 2020, 2024
articles.authors: Gary Johnson, Spencer Cragun, Jake Yoder
articles.abstract: Post‐2024, the United States faces an acute labor crisis marked by accelerating Local Election Official (LEO) attrition. This study examines causal drivers of this exodus, focusing specifically on disproportionate turnover within volatile “swing” and “pivot” counties. Utilizing a mixed‐methods design, using longitudinal data from the Bipartisan Policy Center, US Census Bureau, Elections Voter Survey, MIT Election Data and Science Lab (MEDSL), and the Reed LEO survey, alongside an original dataset compiled from 74 competitive counties and 25 “super landslide” counties. Using Geographic Information Systems, we connect a detailed county profile to spatial mapping of the legal and political environment across the 2016, 2020, and 2024 elections. LEOs in highly competitive jurisdictions face an erosion of institutional trust, serving as a primary catalyst for departure. These volatile jurisdictions highlight where democratic machinery is vulnerable, offering evidence‐based insights for state‐level policy interventions designed to stabilize the public administrative workforce amidst unprecedented hyperpolarization.

articles.title: Governing Before the State: Indigenous Javanese Administrative Theory
articles.abstract: Public administration scholarship often treats the Weberian ideal type as a universal model of bureaucracy, making governance arrangements that differ from it appear deficient rather than different. A decolonizing approach instead asks whether non‐Western historical records can offer alternative ways of theorizing governance. This study explores that possibility through the Nagarakretagama, a 14th‐century Javanese court eulogy composed by Mpu Prapanca in 1365, which predates Machiavelli's The Prince by 148 years. Qualitative content analysis of all 98 cantos identifies five governance domains: bureaucratic hierarchy, mandala‐based territorial administration, conditional fiscal exemptions, a legal order combining written law and custom, and ceremonial practices integrated with administration. These dimensions show how the Javanese empire organized authority, territory, revenue, law, and legitimacy through institutional arrangements that differ from the Weberian model. Reading this governance system as theory reveals an alternative conceptualization of administration and advances a decolonizing, pluriversal approach to public administration.

articles.title: Democratic Backsliding and Governance Outcomes: Measuring Administrative and Political Channels of Decline
articles.abstract: Democratic backsliding has emerged as a defining political challenge of the contemporary era, yet systematic cross‐national evidence linking it to governance outcomes remains scarce. This article argues that backsliding affects governance through two analytically distinct channels: a political accountability channel, whereby weakened contestation and oversight reduce the external costs of poor performance; and an administrative channel, through which executive politicization erodes meritocratic recruitment and bureaucratic impartiality. Using a country‐year panel of 86 countries from 1996 to 2024 and generalized structural equation models, we decompose the direct, indirect, and total effects of backsliding on government effectiveness, regulatory quality, and control of corruption across stages of democratic decline. The findings show that governance deterioration is stage‐specific, channel‐specific, and outcome‐specific, following a nonlinear, U‐shaped pattern in which complete erosion—rather than autocratic reversion—produces the largest governance losses.

articles.title: Organizational Design for Public Managers By Mary E.Guy, Irvine, CA: Melvin & Leigh, Publishers, 2025. 208 pp. $44.95. ISBN : 979‐8‐99‐293050‐4
To Add Insult to Injury: Exploring the Impact of Policy Inequity on Administrative Burden
articles.authors: Yongzheng Yang, Qingqing Zhang, Peng Liu
articles.abstract: The relationship between inequity and administrative burden constitutes a pivotal concern in the realm of public administration and policy, but how policy inequity (i.e., inequity in policy implementation) influences administrative burden has garnered scant attention. The present study employs data about public assistance programs in China spanning from 2015 to 2017 to examine the consequences of policy inequity on administrative burden. The empirical findings underscore that policy inequity augments psychological and compliance costs while concurrently diminishing citizens' participation in welfare programs, thereby indicating that policy inequity intensifies administrative burden. Notably, individual‐level social capital and contextual‐level information transparency in terms of public exposure related to welfare approval and receipt significantly moderate this relationship. Contrary to our theoretical expectations, social capital and public exposure amplify, rather than dampen, the impact of policy inequity on administrative burden. This study highlights the policy inequity lens and offers important implications for burden reduction.

articles.title: Expansive Public Service Delivery: Advancing Public Value Governance
articles.authors: Mary K. Feeney, Julie Langer, Justin M. Stritch
articles.abstract: Public administration has traditionally emphasized the normative ideal that public agencies have a responsibility to improve the lives of communities through public service delivery. We turn to public libraries to explore possibilities for what we call Expansive Public Service Delivery. Expansive Public Service Delivery is defined by a mission to serve all, professional and ethical responsibilities, and proactive responsiveness through outreach and (re)assessment. Public libraries have long aimed to improve communities and advance democracy by providing open, free information access to all. Today, they also proactively seek to expand their services to underserved groups ensuring their relevance and mission achievement. This research draws from 25 in‐depth qualitative interviews to explore librarian narratives to identify four core responsibilities that constitute Expansive Public Service Delivery. We conclude with a discussion of how service for all, professionalism, ethical responsibility, and reflexive decision‐making around community needs can result in more vibrant, sustainable public organizations.

articles.title: An Experimental Comparison of AI-Enabled Semi-Structured Interviews and Fixed Surveys: Respondent Satisfaction, Response Patterns, Quality, and Representation
articles.authors: Amanda Austin, Edward Hohe, Ryan Kennedy, Leib Litman, William Minozzi, Laura Moses
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) interviewing offers the potential to enhance the depth and quality of survey research, yet it may also introduce respondent fatigue and unintended consequences for the measurement of political attitudes. From the standpoint of respondents, more extensive interviews impose greater cognitive and temporal burdens, which may reduce engagement or increase satisficing. From the perspective of political behavior researchers, deeper probing may shift the subset of beliefs or arguments that respondents access when forming opinions, thereby altering the distribution and apparent stability of measured attitudes. To investigate these dynamics, we conduct a large-scale, fully randomized experiment. We find that AI-mediated interviewing significantly increases both the volume and specificity of respondents’ articulated rationales, but any decline in participant satisfaction is minuscule and we detect no increase in participant rolloff. However, AI interviews appear to shape subsequent responses: After offering justifications through AI interaction, respondents exhibit greater polarization in follow-up items. This result suggests that AI interviewing may alter the cognitive architecture of opinion formation. These findings both highlight the potential for AI interviewing and underscore the need for studies of how AI interviewing may become a source of attitudinal change.

articles.title: Attitudes Toward Energy Across European Union Member States (2006–2024)
articles.authors: Piotr Jabkowski, Mariusz Baranowski, Piotr Cichocki
articles.abstract: Our study describes European attitudes toward energy using a harmonized dataset comprising 46 waves of the Eurobarometer (2006–2024). This tracking survey covers all European Union member states; hence, our data accumulates 1,286 individual country surveys. We focus on attitudes relevant to energy transition through three complementary lenses: energy issue salience, policy priorities, and opinions on renewable energy sources. This study documents cross-national and temporal variation in attitudes without estimating the causal effects of specific energy-related European policies or contextual events. We record a marked increase in the salience of energy during crisis periods, especially Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, which rapidly elevated energy’s importance in the hierarchy of public concerns. We also show that support for renewables, in the context of energy transition, coexists with affordability and security concerns in some regions of the EU, particularly in Central-Eastern and Southern Europe. To our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically harmonize such a large collection of Eurobarometer waves into a single comparable dataset, enabling long-term tracking of energy attitudes across all EU member states. In addition to the substantive results, our study also points to several difficulties the Eurobarometer project faces in providing long-term monitoring of public opinion across the highly diverse member states of the European Union.

articles.title: The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income: Experimental Evidence from Two U.S. States
articles.authors: Eva Vivalt, Elizabeth Rhodes, Alexander Bartik, David Broockman, Patrick Krause, Sarah Miller
articles.abstract: We study the causal impacts of income on a rich array of employment outcomes, leveraging an experiment in which 1,000 low-income individuals were randomized into receiving $1,000 per month unconditionally for three years, with a control group of 2,000 participants receiving $50/month. We gather detailed survey data, administrative records, and data from a mobile phone app. The transfer caused total individual income excluding the transfers to fall by about $1,900/year relative to the control group and a 4.2 percentage point decrease in labor market participation. Participants reduced their work hours as a result of the transfers by 1-2 hours/week and participants’ partners reduced their work hours by a comparable amount. Among other categories of time use, the greatest increase generated by the transfer was in time spent on leisure. Despite asking detailed questions about amenities, we find no impact on quality of employment, and our confidence intervals can rule out even small improvements. Treated participants broadly increase expenditures, led by spending on non-durable goods and services, with smaller increases in spending on durable goods and human capital. We observe no significant effects on degree attainment, though the magnitudes of the estimated effects generally appear larger among younger participants. Measures of subjective well-being are higher among treated participants in the first year of the transfers but then revert to control group levels. Overall, our results suggest a moderate labor supply effect that does not appear offset by other productive activities.

articles.title: China’s solar expansion policy reduces bird diversity
articles.authors: Huiming Zhang, Aixin Zhang, Kai Wu, Yinyin Cai, Shanjun Li, Shouyang Wang, Yueming (Lucy) Qiu, Shoujun Huang, Thi Thuc Anh Phan
articles.abstract: Could the global transition to renewable energy create a green dilemma that pits carbon reduction against biodiversity conservation? This study examined the effect of policies promoting solar photovoltaics on local avian biodiversity using a panel dataset covering 2344 counties in China from 2014 to 2023. Policies that favored photovoltaic expansion led to reductions in bird diversity, disproportionately affecting wealthier and nondesert regions, as well as widespread species. The mechanism operated primarily through land conversion: Cropland and grassland were transformed into developed areas, reducing the diversity of vegetation. Paradoxically, the leaf area index increased, a pattern we term “inferior greening,” whereby diverse natural landscapes were replaced by dense but ecologically homogeneous vegetation. We argue that future photovoltaic development should be accompanied by strict biodiversity safeguards, especially in economically developed regions with high habitat complexity.

articles.title: Beneath consensus: political framing of gender-based violence in the Italian press, 2005–2023
articles.abstract: Discourse on gender-based violence started as a political struggle driven by feminist movements allied with progressive parties in the 1970s. However, in recent years, both progressive and conservative Italian parties have proposed and approved laws to combat gender-based violence. The combination of cross-partisan legislation and sharp cultural divisions makes Italy an interesting case for examining how polarization can persist alongside legislative consensus. This study draws on a large corpus of newspaper articles (7,978) from progressive, moderate, and conservative national outlets to address the following questions: How did the distribution of frames of gender-based violence vary across the political spectrum between 2005 and 2023 (ideological polarization)? Did newspapers make explicit adversarial claims against the opposing political side (affective polarization), and if so, around which frames? Combining Structural Topic Modeling and qualitative content analysis, this article shows that the salience of gender-based violence increased across the political spectrum. However, ideological polarization persists regarding how newspapers describe gender-based violence and which solutions they privilege, with progressives increasingly focusing on preventive, rather than punitive, interventions. At the same time, gender-based violence became a catalyst for deep partisan divisions around gender identity and immigration, two discursive overlaps that fuel affective polarization. By examining the framing process as a site of both ideological and affective polarization, this study bridges the literatures on social problems and political polarization and provides a data-driven understanding about the actual content of opposing positions.

articles.title: Multiracial young adults’ experiences of Whiteness as a wage and tax
articles.abstract: Debates persist on the racial position of multiracial Americans, namely whether this population will “become White” or not. However, the premise of this question is predicated on a monoracial paradigm of race that cannot fully account for the experiences of multiracial individuals. Multiracial experiences with Whiteness, including ways they conform to and confound monoracial expectations, have the potential to reshape our understandings of racial constructions, boundaries, and futures, particularly considering shifting racial demographics. One necessary precursor toward these insights lies in the distinctions between how multiracial and monoracial individuals experience Whiteness. Drawing on thirty-seven in-depth interviews with multiracial young adults with White ancestry in the Midwest, I argue that multiracial individuals experience Whiteness as a wage (privileges) and a tax (costs). Like monoracial Whites, multiracial individuals viewed as White can receive public and psychological wages, yet these wages are offset by an inseparable “racial tax,” which is predicated on the contingent and exclusive nature of Whiteness. These results underscore the utility of calling attention to the monoracial structure, as well as recognizing and theorizing beyond its limits.

articles.title: Review of “Fighting for a Foothold: How Government and Markets Undermine Black Middle-Class Suburbia”
Defended neighborhoods, vulnerable routines: routine activities, collective efficacy, and the social ecology of discrimination
articles.authors: Nicolo P Pinchak, Christopher R Browning, Bethany Boettner, J Brandon Carter, Catherine A Calder
articles.abstract: We describe hypotheses about how features of urban settings—including location types, sociodemographic composition, and the extent of collective efficacy (CE)—are differentially related to Black and White individuals’ risks of experiencing discrimination while conducting routine activities. These hypotheses are then tested with data from a large, representative sample of caregivers in the Adolescent Health and Development in Context study (2014–2016). We find that Black individuals are twice as likely as White individuals to report experiencing discrimination in their routine activities, and this Black-White gap is further increased among workplaces, grocery stores, and businesses relative to other locations. Additionally, Black and White individuals report similarly increased probabilities of experiencing discrimination at schools. Consistent with an extension of research on “defended neighborhoods,” exposure to higher CE is positively associated with discrimination for Black individuals especially among areas high in socioeconomic status or high in proportion White population. However, for White individuals, exposure to higher CE is negatively associated with discrimination especially among areas low in socioeconomic status or low in proportion White population. This study underscores that measuring social processes at routine activity settings, rather than just in home neighborhoods, is essential for research on everyday well-being. Further, the findings complement calls to invest in the resource capacity of high-poverty and low-proportion White neighborhoods.

articles.title: When hazards don’t make law: structural resonance in global disaster-law diffusion, 1960–2025
articles.abstract: This article asks why states adopt comprehensive national disaster laws. Rather than treating legislation as an automatic response to hazard exposure, we conceptualize disaster-law adoption as a process of structural resonance: regional diffusion pressures become consequential when they align with domestic governance needs and administrative capacity. Using a new country-year dataset of first adoptions across 204 states and territories from 1960 to 2025, we estimate Cox proportional hazards models with multiple imputation. Recent hazard exposure predicts adoption only in simpler specifications and loses significance once diffusion and state-structure variables are introduced. Regional adoption share strongly accelerates first adoption. Decentralization and government accountability are also associated with earlier enactment, and regional diffusion is amplified in more decentralized polities. The findings show that disaster legalization is not simply a functional response to risk. It is a sociological process in which external legal templates gain force where domestic authority is fragmented and the demand for administrative coordination is high.

articles.title: Explaining gendered language through embedding approximation: how “stupid” became a man’s word
articles.abstract: Recent advances in word embedding have reinvigorated macro-historical cultural analysis based on empirical data. However, these methods primarily model the semantic structure of language, which can obscure the pragmatic dimension of language use central to sociology. Focusing on a previous study of “unintelligence” words in 20th-century American discourse, I investigate the puzzling finding that these words became more male-aligned over time. I argue there is a one-to-many mapping between low-level distance in the embedding space and high-level cultural meanings, and reconsider the stereotype-based interpretation of the changing gender alignment of “unintelligence” words. While the gender axis reliably measures gendered associations, distance-based associations do not neatly map onto well-defined gender stereotypes. Cross-validating embedding alignments against direct co-occurrence with gender-identity words, I first demonstrate that the masculinization of “unintelligence” is unlikely to be driven by judgments directed at gendered persons. Applying an adapted A La Carte (ALC) approximation of individual context words and sentences, I then characterize the pragmatic register of the influential context words—their tone and stance—through close reading validated against the NRC Emotion Lexicon: the contexts driving masculinization shifted from affiliative ease (“soft” contexts, e.g., “adored,” “wholesome”) toward confrontational intensity (“harsh” contexts, e.g., “sin,” “shout”). Robustness checks across randomly sampled word sublists confirm that this pragmatic register shift, not changing judgments of male intellect, is associated with the masculinization. This study demonstrates the interpretive gap in embedding-based methods and calls for more rigorous approaches to intersubjectively valid interpretation of cultural change.

articles.title: Review of “Detroit Never Left: Black Space, White Borders, Latino Crossings”
Festivalized marriage as a Time Threshold: Spring Festival bottlenecks, Qualification Audits, and escalating entry standards in rural China
articles.authors: Yong Yu, Keke Qin, Wenzhao Huang, Shishi Tang
articles.abstract: When do institutional calendars become stratifying devices rather than neutral schedules of action? Drawing on two Spring Festival windows in villages under Yingchunting Subdistrict, Wugang, Hunan, this article shows that rural bachelors’ marriage seeking becomes festivalized: compressed into a recurrent return window where families, matchmakers, and prospective spouses assemble evidence, compare candidates, and clear outcomes before migrants disperse. We theorize Spring Festival as a Time Threshold: a window-deadline-clearing structure that synchronizes dispersed actors and converts courtship into concentrated evaluation. Inside this threshold, a Qualification Audit makes hypergamy auditable by translating marriageability and county-seat mobility into evidence bundles of housing, renovation progress, cash flow, bridewealth timing, parental backstops, reputation, and interactional fit. The window also creates Outcome Filing and Threshold Escalation: advancement, suspension, ghosting, and failure travel as records that alter next-cycle starting positions and evidentiary demands. Combining 114 interviews with 94 participants, 224 hours of observation, 41 reconstructed chains, and 297 de-identified artifacts, the article specifies when calendars stratify: recurrent deadlines, synchronized availability, high-stakes qualification, portable evidence, and outcomes that travel. The mechanism speaks beyond rural China to admissions cycles, visa windows, hiring seasons, and other institutional calendars that convert unequal life chances into auditable records with cumulative consequences.

articles.title: Countering the Current: Flood Risk and Uneven Patterns of Immobility
articles.abstract: Highlights Increased neighborhood flood risk predicts lower odds of households moving out of their neighborhood. This association is largest for renters, low-income homeowners, and Black homeowners. This pattern may reflect housing insecurity, which can manifest as both immobility and instability. Studies of climate and population should disaggregate by race and ethnicity, income, and housing tenure.

articles.title: The Glass Is Half Full: The Safety Net for Low-Income Women Around Childbirth
articles.authors: Colleen Heflin, Taryn W. Morrissey, Hyojeong Kim
articles.abstract: Highlights Employed, social welfare–connected mothers experience a substantial reduction in earnings around a child's birth. Social welfare programs, assuming full take-up, can offset these lost earnings after birth but not during pregnancy. Most social welfare benefits available around birth are nutrition assistance, which are not fungible. These mothers spend about six months out of the labor force, with Black mothers returning earlier, on average.

articles.title: Youth Subjective Life Expectancy and Early Labor Market Choices
articles.abstract: Highlights Survival beliefs elicited at ages 18–26 predict later pension contributions. A 1-SD-higher life expectancy is linked to 5% more pension wealth 15 years later. Job formality, not labor force participation, drives most of the pension gap. This SLE–pension link grows over the life cycle, from 2.5–5% at ages 18–26 to 9–11% at ages 48–52.

articles.title: Benjamin Franklin and Democratic Education Beyond Schooling
articles.abstract: Political theorists have long focused their understanding of democratic education on the institution of the school, particularly the public school, to the exclusion of broader visions of education beyond schooling. But as criticisms of schooling from outside the academy mount, it becomes imperative to examine the origins of American educational thought to determine whether opposition to schooling has an older historical source. This essay locates the roots of school skepticism in an alternative American educational tradition beginning with Benjamin Franklin that drew on Locke’s pedagogical arguments to devalue institutional schooling in favor of self-education. Franklin’s educational vision harnessed the independence of the young in early America by incentivizing learning through friendship and self-interest, and resorted to schools only as a guardrail against the abuse of freedom, incorporating them but minimizing their role in education. In this, Franklin initiated the Americanization of Lockean pedagogy, or the school-skeptical tradition in American thought.

articles.title: A theory of political divergence and gradual institutional change
articles.abstract: Why do some societies succeed in breaking away from historical traditions while others remain trapped? This paper proposes a formal theory to investigate the interaction between short‐run and long‐run political dynamics, highlighting a co‐evolution of political institutions and social structures. A society consists of various social groups, such as the rulers, the elites, and the commoners. Short‐run strategic considerations give rise to different coalitions among these groups, which determine not only political regimes but also redistribution policies. In the long run, these policies shape the accumulation of wealth and power, where small initial differences can lead to divergent paths of development. Finally, the paper examines three historical case studies on medieval Europe, imperial China, and the medieval Muslim world to illustrate potential pathways of long‐run political development.

articles.title: Captured participatory institutions: Theory and evidence from Venezuela's Consejos Comunales
articles.abstract: Can participatory institutions (PIs) facilitate development when captured by the government? We propose an original theoretical framework to investigate how changing incumbent priorities can shape the developmental and political effects of captured PIs. While patrons concerned with survival can force PIs to specialize in political activities, those pursuing regime consolidation may incentivize PIs to multitask, delivering developmental gains and political rewards. We deploy our framework to study Venezuela's Communal Councils. Leveraging difference‐in‐differences analyses, an original survey of Council participants, and 51 interviews with government officials and grassroots Communal Council members, we find that Councils yielded both economic and political returns during an early period marked by political stability and regime consolidation. However, as Venezuela's economic collapse pushed the government into an authoritarian survival mode, Councils became politically specialized. While showing that captured PIs can foster development under certain circumstances, our findings cast doubt on PIs’ development‐enhancing potential under autocracy.

articles.title: What Do We Mean by Transparency? Conceptualizing and Operationalizing Transparency in Communication
articles.authors: Wenjia Yan, Li Crystal Jiang, Yiqian Gao, Pingping Jia
articles.abstract: By analyzing 164 articles from communication journals published between 2002 and 2024, this scoping review systematically investigates temporal trends, conceptualizations, and operationalizations of transparency research within communication studies. The analysis identifies three primary conceptual dimensions of transparency: (1) information, encompassing both visibility and interpretation; (2) relations, functioning as an intermediary between dialogue and power; (3) values and norms, reflecting the tensions between ethical ideals and institutional constraints. Operationalization of transparency has predominantly relied on informational measures, whereas relational and value-based dimensions remain comparatively underdeveloped. Increasing attention has been directed toward subjective stakeholder perceptions, emphasizing transparency as a dynamic and context-dependent construct. Overall, the findings indicate that transparency extends beyond a stable informational attribute to incorporate relational and normative functions, while its enactment remains fluid, contextually shaped, and susceptible to unintended consequences.

articles.title: Marital Dissolution, Repartnering, and the Realization of Fertility Desires in Sub‐Saharan Africa
articles.abstract: Women who experience union disruption in sub‐Saharan Africa tend to have lower fertility than those in stable unions. It remains unclear, however, whether this pattern reflects lower fertility desires, constrained opportunities to achieve desired fertility, or both. Using Demographic Health Survey data from 34 countries, this study examines whether fertility differences between women in intact unions and those who experience marital dissolution are primarily driven by differences in family size ideals, unrealized fertility, or unwanted fertility. Results indicate that unrealized fertility is widespread and especially pronounced among women whose first unions ended, particularly those not in union. Although remarriage offers some fertility recovery, it rarely eliminates the reproductive disadvantage associated with union disruption. In contrast, women in intact first unions have higher levels of unwanted fertility across most countries, contributing to the fertility gap. Although women in intact unions have somewhat higher ideal numbers of children than women outside of unions, constrained realization of fertility goals emerges as the dominant factor explaining observed differences. Furthermore, women who experience union dissolution are more likely to revise their desires downward or express uncertainty about future childbearing. These findings underscore the importance of union trajectories in shaping fertility variation in sub‐Saharan Africa.

articles.title: Does Exposure to Community Violence Predict Higher Suicide Rates? The Case of Mexico
articles.abstract: Despite both homicide and suicide being identified as global public health concerns, it is unclear whether and how homicide trends could shape suicide patterns, particularly in low‐or‐middle income countries. We use the case of Mexico, an upper‐middle‐income country that experienced a dramatic increase in homicide after a shift in drug‐enforcement policy in 2006, to evaluate the relationship between community violence and suicide. Our analysis relies on geocoded death certificates microdata for the entire national territory to assess the association between homicide rates and suicide rates at the municipality level for the 2000–2019 period. We find evidence of positive associations between homicide rates and suicide within six months of exposure to high homicide levels, and especially in the period immediately after homicide spikes relative to the violence baseline in the previous three years. These surges in suicide are primarily driven by auto‐inflicted strangulation. No changes in suicide were identified after more than six months of exposure to high homicide levels, or as exposure to increasing homicides accumulated in the long term. Our results are consistent with violence spikes predicting an instant but transitory increase in suicide, plausibly by causing acute fear, stress, and uncertainty in the period immediately surrounding drastic surges in violence.

articles.title: Demographic Structure and Democracy: Population Aging and Immigration in Global Perspective
articles.abstract: Substantial demographic and democratic changes have unfolded globally in recent history, inviting inquiry into the relationship between these two phenomena. Joining the growing research in political demography, we advance a conceptual framework that links structural demographic factors to democratic progress and decline through economic, ideological, and representational mechanisms. Guided by this framework, we analyze two key demographic factors using an original longitudinal dataset covering 153 countries from 1975 to 2020. The results demonstrate a nonlinear and context‐dependent relationship between demography and democracy. Specifically, population aging and immigration levels are generally associated with lower levels of democracy; though in the case of immigration, this relationship weakens as immigrant shares increase, indicating a nonlinear pattern. Importantly, demography is not destiny: the relationship between population structure and democracy is further shaped by economic and political contexts. Overall, this paper underscores the profound and nuanced ways in which structural demographic change shapes democratic outcomes.

articles.title: Value Change and the New Wave of Fertility Postponement in Western Europe
articles.authors: Oskar Lindström, Raffaele Guetto, Daniele Vignoli
articles.abstract: Since 2010, Western Europe has experienced a renewed wave of fertility postponement, contributing to declining fertility rates and rising childlessness. Although multiple explanations have been proposed, the role of ideational factors remains underexplored. This study examines whether broad changes in values help explain contemporary fertility postponement, drawing on the framework of the Second Demographic Transition (SDT). We apply Schwartz's theory of basic human values to investigate trends in openness‐to‐change and conservation among women of childbearing age, assessing both aggregate changes over time and individual‐level associations with having entered parenthood. Results show that these values are strongly associated with differences in entry into motherhood. However, the stability in value orientations over time suggests that values are unlikely to be a primary driver of the recent fertility postponement trend. Moreover, the relationship between values and entry into motherhood has remained unchanged, indicating that contemporary postponement extends across value orientations. Some regional heterogeneity emerges, with Southern Europe showing value shifts that may contribute to fertility postponement, though their overall influence appears limited. We conclude that broad shifts in SDT‐related values are unlikely to explain the widespread fertility decline observed in Western Europe.

Contested Rule Formation Under Institutional Mismatch: A Framework for Early‐Phase Governance of Disruptive Innovations
articles.abstract: Disruptive innovations often diffuse faster than inherited policy institutions can classify, assign jurisdiction, and govern them. In these early phases, the central struggle is often not yet about the stringency of substantive standards, but about prior questions of what the innovation is (its legal and administrative classification), who is competent to decide (allocation of jurisdiction and decision authority), and where authoritative decisions should be made (designation of legitimate governance venues). This article develops Contested Rule Formation (CRF), a meso‐level, four‐stage framework for analyzing early‐phase governance under institutional mismatch in institutionally dense settings. CRF reconceptualizes institutional voids as localized misfit along five co‐evolving dimensions: recognition, authority, enforcement capacity, venue clarity, and interpretive frames. It then specifies a staged mechanism (incipient recognition, exploratory tactics, rule crystallization, and consolidation/backlash) in which classification and jurisdictional settlements function as rate‐limiting gates for durable rulemaking and for procedural learning, understood as a contingent trajectory rather than an automatic result of contestation. A proof‐of‐concept comparison of ride‐hailing governance in California and Austin/Texas shows how different category‐and‐venue pathways shaped early outcomes. The article closes with a diagnostic and comparative research agenda for studying upstream governance across AI, fintech, energy, and other domains of disruptive innovation and socio‐technical change.

articles.title: Climate-Related South–South Migration in the Pacific Islands Region: Assessing Regional, Subregional, and Bilateral Governance Frameworks
articles.abstract: Climate change is reshaping population movements within and between Pacific Island Countries and Territories (PICTs), exposing critical gaps in how international migration is understood and governed in the Pacific. This study assesses key regional, subregional, and bilateral agreements in the Pacific to understand how they engage with climate mobility and to identify areas of neglect. It highlights a novel finding: while population movements between Pacific islands are a longstanding reality in the region, existing governance frameworks have so far rarely addressed climate-related South–South migration between PICTs. As a result, the needs of vulnerable receiving communities within PICTs have been largely overlooked in both research and policy. The paper further argues that this oversight reflects broader Global North biases in migration scholarship and governance that continue to shape orthodox understandings of climate-related mobility commonly framed through South to North migration paradigms. By centering South–South dynamics in the Pacific, a region often marginalized in global migration research, this study contributes to efforts to decenter dominant migration frameworks and calls for more inclusive approaches to climate-related migration scholarship and governance that reflect Pacific realities and the perspectives of affected communities.

articles.title: Age at First Marriage or Cohabitation Among First-, Second-, and 2.5-Generation Immigrant Women, Finland 1987–2020
articles.authors: Citlali Trigos-Raczkowski, Kelsey Q. Wright, Joonas Pitkänen, Silvia Loi, Pekka Martikainen, Heta Moustgaard, Mikko Myrskylä
articles.abstract: Immigrants and their descendants are increasingly forming families across Europe, yet little is known about how immigration background shapes first union entry in emerging immigration contexts. Here, we examine whether immigrant generation, age at arrival, and sending region are associated with entry into opposite-sex first unions for women in Finland from 1987 to 2020. Treating cohabitation and direct marriage as competing events, we estimate cause-specific hazards in separate accelerated failure time models. We find a systematic bifurcation in union entry: while nearly all immigrant groups forgo the modal Finnish path of first entering a nonmarital cohabitation, specific subgroups—including the second generation, first generation arriving during adolescence, and women from the Former Soviet Union, Eastern Europe, North America, South Asia, and the Middle East and North Africa—exhibit accelerated transitions to direct marriage. While these findings demonstrate heterogeneity in the pathways by which immigrant women enter unions, with no single narrative of delay or convergence capturing the full picture, the overall pattern of later and less cohabitation and higher levels of direct marriage suggest that immigrant women face substantively different cultural, institutional, and social capital conditions than nonimmigrant women.

Same neighbourhood, same employer? Residential proximity and workplace concentration among immigrants
articles.authors: JooHee Han, Are Skeie Hermansen, Aleksander Å Madsen, Mats Lillehagen
articles.abstract: Living near one another can channel immigrants toward workplaces through social connections and information flow, shared local opportunity structures, and other residentially patterned pathways, yet few studies link residential proximity to employment outcomes among immigrants and their children. Using Norwegian linked employer–employee administrative data with detailed residential locations, we study how neighbourhood co-residence is tied to workplace concentration and individual wages among coworkers of immigrant and native background. We compare observed co-employment of neighbours against a simulated baseline of random workplace allocation within municipalities and adjust for stable local geography using neighbourhood fixed effects. We find that immigrants are considerably more likely than natives living in the same neighbourhood to work with immigrant neighbours, particularly coethnics from the same country of origin. Immigrant neighbour exposure concentrates workers in low-wage, immigrant-dense establishments but is only modestly tied to wages, suggesting that such pathways may reinforce workplace segregation without clear individual economic costs or benefits. Children of immigrants, in contrast, are not overexposed to immigrant-background neighbours at work compared with natives. These patterns tie residential proximity to immigrants’ workplace concentration in ways consistent with neighbourhood-based network mechanisms, while weaker links in the second generation point to broader integration into the mainstream economy.

articles.title: Rethinking Risk Society from the Global South: On the Unequal Distribution of Risk
articles.abstract: Beck’s theory of risk society offers a powerful account of manufactured uncertainty, transboundary hazards, and the limits of national and class-based insulation under reflexive modernization. Yet its universalizing language remains insufficient for explaining how risks are differentially produced, displaced, governed, and lived across colonial and postcolonial geographies. This article critically reconstructs Beck from the standpoint of the Global South, understood not as a fixed geography but as a historically produced positionality within unequal global power relations. I argue that the key issue is not whether risks become transboundary but how unequal capacities for protection, buffering, accountability, and repair stabilize asymmetrical exposure under global interdependence. To address this, I propose the concept of unequal risk regimes , through which accumulation logics, spatial displacement, slow violence, and institutional–epistemic mechanisms combine to routinize and obscure harm. Beck’s theory should not be abandoned; rather, it should be transformed through a justice- and mechanism-oriented sociology of global risk.

articles.title: The Consent to Destroy: Imperial Melancholia and the Hegemony of Fragmentation
articles.abstract: Across the world’s most powerful states, millions actively embrace the destruction of the shared reality on which democratic life depends. Democracy does not simply collapse from without; it can be unmade from within through consent. This article introduces hegemonic fragmentation, an original concept revealing how declining empires manufacture consent for their own unraveling. Synthesizing Arendt’s analysis of the common world with Hall’s theory of hegemonic consent, I generate a novel framework to identify the culturally constructed consent for the dissolution of shared factuality, political space, and meaning, experienced not as loss but as freedom and belonging. Imperial melancholia, the refusal to mourn lost dominance, is the affective mechanism converting structural decline into the desire to destroy. Through conjunctural comparison of Trump’s United States and Putin’s Russia, I reveal authoritarian populism as a pathological sociological mechanism through which imperial decline is distorted into consent to destroy the common world.

articles.title: The first 4 years: evolution of community attitudes towards refugees in a new rural resettlement location in Australia
articles.authors: Susan E Watt, Stefania Paolini, Tadgh McMahon
articles.abstract: This study examined the evolution of host community attitudes towards refugees in the first 4 years of a new rural resettlement location. We used threat, contact, and attribution theories to obtain a dynamic picture of responses to refugee settlement. Six telephone surveys with host community adults (N = 1,132) gathered cross-sectional and longitudinal data. Attitudes towards refugees became increasingly positive, perceived threats declined, intergroup contact initially grew and then decreased (during the pandemic), and the host community became more positive regarding the refugee intake numbers. Neighbours were perceived as more likely to help one another, and multicultural neighbourhoods were perceived as getting along increasingly well, although with a drop from 2020 to 2021. Interestingly, contact outcomes were attributed to refugees rather than self or circumstances. National survey data confirmed the changes did not reflect broader trends. These results demonstrate that even in less diverse rural areas, positive intergroup dynamics can develop, challenging stereotypes of closed-mindedness and resistance to newcomers.

articles.title: Three Configurations of In‐House Government Consulting: Public‐Value Purpose and Organizational Viability
articles.abstract: Governments have created in‐house consulting organizations to reduce dependence on external firms and retain public capability and control. Yet organizations grouped under this label pursue different forms of public value that require different designs. This article distinguishes three reasons for a dedicated unit: retaining control over consequential work, capturing returns from problems that recur across government, and mobilizing expertise dispersed across public and adjacent institutions. It develops three corresponding configurations—Strategic Transformation, Scalable Solutions, and Expertise Platform—and shows how choices about work, staffing, knowledge, authority, client relationships, financing, and evaluation must fit together. Documentary comparison of eight units in five countries grounds the analysis. The cases show that viability depends on whether work renews the conditions needed for subsequent work and that evaluation must reflect configuration and stage. Internalization is therefore organization‐building, not the reversal of a procurement decision: a unit creates public value only when work reproduces the conditions on which that value depends.

articles.title: Conditional Compliance: The Role of Sector and Policy Design in State Sexual Misconduct Policy
articles.authors: Jaeyeong Nam, Daniel L Fay, Emily Boykin, Elizabeth Bell
articles.abstract: The role of principal-agent dynamics in performance and accountability reforms has been a recurring theme in public administration research. Yet, less attention has been dedicated to how the intersection of sector and policy design shapes principal-agent dynamics and subsequent policy outcomes. This study theoretically explores and empirically tests how sector and policy design shape the effects of state legislation that seeks to prevent shirking (mismanagement and underreporting) in the context of sexual misconduct outcomes in U.S. colleges and universities. We code every state policy designed to regulate higher education institutions’ management of sexual misconduct from 2007 to 2018 in the U.S. and leverage a Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood with a staggered difference-in-differences design to identify the effects. Our findings suggest that both sector and policy design matter: public institutions increase reporting in response to prevention policies that promote education and awareness, but prevention policies have no effect on private institutions. Other policies regulating enforcement and infrastructure produce null effects across both sectors. These findings have important implications for principal-agent theory and policy design research on effective methods for reducing shirking in social equity, accountability, and performance reporting.

articles.title: Governing Party Issue Ownership and How Citizens Assess Conditions
articles.abstract: It is well-documented that Americans perceive conditions more favorably when their preferred party is in power. This study considers a second, more subtle, but potentially impactful partisan bias: that the governing party’s policy reputations lead voters to perceive better conditions on the issues it “owns.” In US politics, voters trust Democrats more on environmental, healthcare, education, and safety net issues while Republicans are favored on immigration, crime, defense, and keeping taxes low. In two studies, I observe whether these reputations also impact perceptions when each party is in power. First, I analyze hundreds of survey toplines from Gallup Trends, dating from 1956 to the present, about public perceptions on a variety of party-owned policy areas. Second, to leverage greater variation in control of subnational government, I analyze seven surveys that ask about state-level conditions as well. While results from the former analysis are only suggestive, both approaches point toward an association between the governing party and how citizens assess conditions on the issues it owns.

articles.title: How Election Fundamentals and Racialized Considerations Shape Asian American Vote Choice Through the Trump Era
articles.authors: Joyce H. Nguy, Nathan K. Chan, Jessica HyunJeong Lee
articles.abstract: Racial minorities voted for Trump at higher rates in 2024 than in previous elections, prompting renewed interest in the factors driving minority vote choice. Here, we focus on Asian Americans, the fastest growing single-race group in the United States. Bridging theories of economic voting and race-centered explanations, we present a comprehensive, up-to-date account of Asian American vote choice through the Trump era. We analyze the 2024, 2020, and 2016 Collaborative Multiracial Post-Election Surveys to assess indicators of Trump support over time among Asian Americans, with comparative analysis of Black, Latino, and White voters ( N = 24,061). We find that economic considerations shaped vote choice in 2024 among Asian Americans, and all other racial groups. Linked fate remained associated with lower Trump support among Asian Americans in 2024, indicating that race continued to matter even years after the peak of anti-Asian hate. In comparison, linked fate also shaped opposition to Trump among Black voters but not Latinos in 2024. Throughout the Trump era, racial resentment among non-Black racial groups and anti-immigrant sentiment among all racial groups consistently predicted greater Trump support, including Asian Americans, despite their predominantly immigrant-origin backgrounds. This research contributes to growing scholarship that addresses conservatism among minoritized communities.

AI and the party: The three faces of party organization and artificial intelligence
articles.authors: Şebnem Yardımcı-Geyikçi, Patricia Correa, Giulia Sandri, Philipp Darius, Jasmin Fitzpatrick, Anne Goldmann, Fabio Lupato, Erdem Yörük, Kristina Weissenbach
articles.abstract: This Research Note explores the emerging intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) and party politics by applying Katz and Mair’s “three faces” framework to analyze the role of AI in reshaping party organization. While AI is not yet uniformly transforming parties, its growing use in campaigning, policymaking, membership engagement, and internal management introduces new dynamics of centralisation, personalisation, and automation. The note highlights both the opportunities AI offers for efficiency and responsiveness, and the risks it poses to transparency, accountability, and democratic representation. It argues that the incorporation of AI into party life is uneven, contested, and mediated by broader political and institutional configurations, and require closer empirical and conceptual scrutiny. In doing so, the paper outlines a new research agenda for understanding how technological change intersects with party transformation in contemporary democracies.

articles.title: Ballots and battlefields: Assessing the impact of the war in Ukraine on voting in the 2022 Italian general election
articles.authors: Claudio Cozzi Fucile, Luciana Fazio, Pierangelo Isernia, Sergio Martini, Paolo Bellucci
articles.abstract: Research on the electoral impact of foreign policy has largely focused on the United States. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine offers an opportunity to reassess this question in a European context. This article examines the role the war in Ukraine played in shaping electoral behaviour in Italy during the September 2022 general elections. Relying on the ITANES pre- and post-electoral survey, we assess whether attitudes toward supporting Ukraine contributed to explaining Italian voter choices. The results indicate that orientations toward the Ukraine war, operationalised as support for both economic sanctions against Russia and military assistance to Ukraine, were associated with voter choice, even though domestic issues, such as immigration, remained more influential in structuring electoral preferences. We argue that this pattern reflects the strategic behaviour of parties in addressing a politically sensitive and potentially divisive issue. The article contributes to the ongoing debate on the electoral relevance of foreign policy by providing new evidence from a critical moment for the European continent.

articles.title: Public support for cordons sanitaires against the radical left and radical right
articles.authors: Alexander Davenport, Jørgen Eikvar Axelsen, Aleš Kudrnáč
articles.abstract: Though radical parties have often been excluded from government by mainstream elites (the ‘cordon sanitaire’), little is known about how voters evaluate such practices. Using data from the Czech Republic, where radical left and radical right parties have both been excluded, we examine voters’ support for the cordon sanitaire, and whether they differentiate between parties in this regard. We find considerable popular support for the cordon sanitaire, with less than a quarter of respondents rejecting this idea outright. Notably, left-wing voters are more likely to oppose cordons sanitaires against both the radical left and right, while right-wing voters are highly supportive of excluding both parties from government, with limited support among the electorate for excluding only one side of the ideological spectrum. The results indicate that where the cordon sanitaire has been established at the elite level, it may garner substantial popular support for excluding a range of radical parties.
