The governance of snarking: Anti-fandom as tiny publics
articles.abstract: This article examines online celebrity ‘snarking’ communities, otherwise known as anti-fandom spaces or even hate forums. Specifically, we provide an analysis of the governance of these groups and how they develop a collective morality through both articulations with the celebrities’ mediation and with the logics of social justice. Using data collected from a digital ethnography of two popular celebrity snark spaces, we employ Critical Discourse Analysis to track the particular discursive repertoires and vernaculars which characterise snark across multiple platforms. We argue that despite the perceived ‘incivility’ of these online spaces, discourses of care, justice and solidarity often emerge which complicate existing narratives of these groups. Though participation in snarking collectives is often explained in pathologising or individualising narratives of anti-fandom, we demonstrate some of the reflexive work that happens in these spaces which sometimes ignites sociological discussions and frustrations at inequalities. We therefore conceptualise snark through the lens of a ‘tiny public’ that identifies and explores broader race and class injustice in contemporary society. Here, the prevailing discourses about celebrity subjects ‘failing upwards’ betrays an anger at elites who do not suffer the same material consequences at times of crisis; though many of these frustrations are misdirected back at the celebrity subject and manifest in a collective desire to see repercussions for the individual celebrity, rather than collective action aimed at the structures that make this failure possible, visible and even lucrative.

articles.title: Exorbitant Privilege of the Periodic Table? Geoeconomics, Endogenous Centrality and Strategic Minerals for the Green Transition,
articles.authors: Josh Kirk, Evgenia Passari, Hélène Rey
articles.abstract: Trade networks underpinning the energy transition are endogenous economic objects, and their structure is a source of market power. Using bilateral trade data for thirteen electrification metals over 1995–2023, we show that trade in these materials has reorganised into a hub-and-spoke system centred on China, in sharp contrast to the more diffuse, multilateral structure of fossil fuels. This centrality did not follow from resource endowments: China holds few of the underlying reserves. It was built through processing investment, industrial policy, and commodity-targeted development finance, an equilibrium outcome rather than a geographical accident. We formalise this logic in a stylised model in which a country chooses how central to become, and show that centrality can map into pricing power: the response of the world price of critical minerals to a supply cut is stronger when the network is more concentrated, the downstream demand and the competitive fringe supply are more inelastic. Constructing text-based, commodity-specific supply shocks and estimating local projections, we find that supply contractions in critical metals raise consumer inflation in the European Union and the United States by roughly twice as much as comparable fossil-fuel shocks, and more persistently. Centrality is therefore not merely a descriptive feature of the new resource map: it can create leverage over global prices. The green transition reduces strategic dependence on hydrocarbon exporters but reconstitutes it around the architecture of mineral supply chains.

articles.title: Drought: Impacts, Prevention, and Adaptation Options Across Scales
articles.authors: Ermias Aynekulu, Gudeta W. Sileshi, Charles N. Wamucii, Mohamed Imam Bakarr, Ulrich Apel, Guadalupe Duron, Daniel Tsegai, Meine van Noordwijk
articles.abstract: Beyond lack of water, drought means that expected levels of water availability are not realized, triggering cascading consequences across land, water, biodiversity, climate, and human systems. Drought reflects variation in water availability, including thresholds, frequency, intensity, duration, and spatial synchrony as well as how expectations and anticipation shape human actions. Drought symptoms are linked to local pressures and broader drivers of change and can induce social and ecological responses. This review synthesizes advances in understanding the biophysical and socioeconomic impacts of drought across temporal scales, from seasonal to multi-year and climatic drought, and across subsystem typologies, including meteorological, hydrological, agricultural, ecological, and socioeconomic drought. The review demonstrates how weakened ecological buffers, governance failures, and policy incoherence intensify drought vulnerability. Building drought resilience requires coordinated action across sectors, scales, and institutions to restore the ecological, social, and governance buffers that sustain human well-being and planetary stability. articles.title: Regime Shifts and Transformations in Social-Ecological Systems: Advancing Critical Frontiers for Safe and Just Futures
articles.authors: Juan C. Rocha, Caroline Schill, Emilie A.L. Lindkvist, Reinette Biggs, Thorsten Blenckner, Anne-Sophie Crépin, Ingo Fetzer, Carl Folke, Amanda Jiménez-Aceituno, Nielja Knecht, Jan J. Kuiper, Steven J. Lade, Carla Lanyon-Garrido, Romi Lotcheris, Romina Martin, Vanessa Masterson, Petr Matous, Michele-Lee Moore, Magnus Nyström, Per Olsson, Laura M. Pereira, Garry Peterson, André Pinto da Silva, Sasha Quahe, Maja Schlüter, Uno Svedin, Lan Wang-Erlandsson, Hannah Zoller
articles.abstract: Current research challenges in sustainability science require us to consider nonlinear changes—shifts that do not happen gradually but can be sudden and difficult to predict. Central questions are therefore how we can prevent harmful shifts, promote desirable ones, and better anticipate both. The regime shifts and transformations literature is well-equipped to address these questions. Yet, even though both research streams stem from the same intellectual roots, they have developed along different paths, with limited exchange between the two, missing opportunities for cross-fertilization. We here review the definitions and history of both research streams to disentangle common grounds and differences. We propose avenues for future research and highlight how stronger integration of both research streams could support the development of more powerful approaches to help us navigate toward safe and just futures.

articles.title: In Pursuit of Spatial, Life‐Course and Social Mobilities: Aspiring Filipino Seafarers Acquiring Migration Ability Through Servitude
articles.abstract: This article examines aspiring Filipino seafarers' pursuit of the triple mobilities : spatial (migration), life course (education to work, youth to adulthood) and social. It focuses on those working as ‘utility cadets’ for manning agencies that supply seafarers to ship operators in exchange for a ship placement. Its aims are twofold. Based on long‐term research and drawing on interviews with utility cadets, successful seafarers who were once utility cadets, and parents or older siblings of utility cadets, it first conceptualises as ability acquisition how aspiring Filipino seafarers turn servitude into a strategy to accumulate the ability to migrate. Second, it shows how this spatial mobility enables their life‐course and social mobilities, and accounts for how these three mobilities are interconnected. The pace of life‐course mobility shaped and was shaped by the degree of the seafarers' contribution to their family's social mobility , and both constituted and were constituted by the seafarers' rank in the seafaring labour hierarchy, which determined their salary. The article further conceptualises the intertwinement of the triple mobilities by explaining their negotiation through processes of convergence and divergence .

articles.title: Reconceptualising Social Integration: Experiences of Internal Youth Migrants in Ghana
articles.authors: Francis Diawuo Darko, Susanne Schech, Udoy Saikia
articles.abstract: Research on migrant social integration has focused mainly on international migration, leaving internal migration, especially in the Global South, underexplored as a site of theory‑building. This paper reconceptualises social integration through an empirical study of young internal migrants in Sunyani, Ghana, a secondary city characterised by informality and decentralised governance. Drawing on a mixed‑methods design of survey data and qualitative narrative interviews, the analysis shows that integration is not a linear or place‑bound outcome but a negotiated process shaped by material precarity, social relations, institutional mediation, and sustained connections to places of origin. While economic participation and co‑ethnic bonding networks enable survival in the informal economy, limited cross‑group trust and exclusionary encounters with local authorities constrain broader inclusion. Importantly, the paper advances translocality as a constitutive dimension of social integration, showing that ongoing obligations to origin communities function as adaptive strategies for managing risk and belonging in contexts of weak urban safety nets, while simultaneously reshaping local embedding. By foregrounding internal migration in a secondary African city, the study challenges state‑centred and settlement‑based integration models and contributes to population geography by reframing social integration as a spatially distributed, relational process within national borders.

articles.title: Deceptive Citizenship as an Instrument of New War: Authoritarian Practices in a Post‐Colonial Context
articles.abstract: The article demonstrates how, under authoritarian practices and post‐colonialism, a state employs deceptive citizenship as an instrument of a ‘new war.’ The deceptive citizenship operates within informational autocracy for a selected category of migrantised people, which make them unaware about the legal, political and mobility consequences of this status. By obscuring the legal, political, and mobility consequences of this status, it enables authorities to symbolically project power beyond territorial boundaries and consolidate their geopolitical post‐colonial standing among citizens. Using Russia's citizenship policies towards displaced Ukrainians between 2014 and 2022 as a case study, this article traces the complex genealogy of these policies and shows how, prior to the full‐scale invasion, they served geopolitical ambitions and postcolonial hegemony. At the same time, it demonstrates that displaced Ukrainians' citizenship practices were driven primarily by the need to cope with uncertainty and insecurity.

articles.title: Neighbourhood Ethnic Diversification in Urban and Rural England and Wales
articles.authors: Richard Wright, Gemma Catney, Mark Ellis, Momoko Nishikido
articles.abstract: The minority ethnic share of the population of England and Wales rose from 8.7% in 2001 to over 18% in 2021. Using 2001, 2011 and 2021 Census data for England and Wales with consistent neighbourhood boundaries, this paper investigates how these aggregate changes translated into alterations in neighbourhood ethnic composition across the urban–rural continuum. We classify neighbourhoods into three diversity types (low, moderate, high) via an entropy‑based metric and track transitions over two decades. Ethnic and racial diversity grew in all neighbourhood types and geographic settings. Between 2001 and 2021, neighbourhoods with all‐White populations all but disappeared, neighbourhoods classified as low diversity with a large White majority declined in number, and counts of moderately diverse neighbourhoods increased. Additionally, the proportion of highly diverse (multiethnic) neighbourhoods tripled during this period. These changes follow a broadly hierarchical pattern, focused first, and most intensively, in London and subsequently occurring in secondary Metropolitan counties and relatively smaller urban settings. Finally, we detect some decade‐specific differences, notably a deceleration in neighbourhood transitions toward greater ethnic diversity between 2011 and 2021. A counterfactual analysis of the consolidation of ethnic diversity into moderately diverse neighbourhoods rather than further condensation into high diversity spaces suggests the rising importance of locational preferences and constraints relative to demographic forces in shaping these new neighbourhood geographies.

articles.title: The Factors Driving Migration Intentions and Destination Preferences in Central, East, and Southeast European Countries
articles.authors: Antea Barišić, Mahdi Ghodsi, Alireza Sabouniha, Robert Stehrer
articles.abstract: This paper studies the determinants of the intentions to emigrate and conditional on migration aspirations, the destination choice in a number of Central East and Southeast European economies (CESEE). Using data from the OeNB Euro Survey, we apply a two‐stage Heckman procedure to identify the drivers of migration intentions – specifically individuals' demographic and household attributes, financial conditions, past economic experiences, and future expectations. In the second stage, conditional on the stated intention to migrate, we examine the determinants of destination choice, distinguishing between EU15, EU‐CEE, and extra‐EU countries. This micro‐level evidence indicates that economic and financial conditions (past, present, and expected) play an important role in shaping migration intentions, while non‐economic factors, including individual demographic and family attributes, as well as network ties, also exert important influence. Destination preferences, conditional on an already existing intention to migrate are not simply a mechanical extension of intention determinants. The choice of the destination region is determined mostly by marital status, educational attainment, and GDP per capita variables in the origin and destination region. This reflects the conceptualisation of migration as a two‐stage decision process, distinguishing between entry into the pool of potential migrants and destination choice within that pool. This stage‐specific perspective thus allows to differentiate determinants of intentions and destination choice of prospective mobility, that empirical results based on actual migration decisions cannot deliver.

articles.title: Household Assets and Internal Mobility in Laos: Agricultural Land, Home Ownership, and Multi‐Stream Population Redistribution
articles.abstract: Internal migration in agrarian economies is usually framed as a rural‐to‐urban transition, but population redistribution follows multiple pathways. Household assets such as land and housing shape these moves, and how they do so is contested: some research finds that assets anchor households in place, while other work finds that they enable movement. This debate has centred on rural‐to‐urban flows in settings of uneven ownership, leaving open how assets relate to the full range of mobility, including non‐migration and rural‐bound moves, where ownership is near‐universal. This study examines that question in Lao PDR, a setting of gradual urbanisation and continued rural dominance. Drawing on the nationally representative Lao Social Indicator Survey, it models three outcomes: migration versus non‐migration, rural versus urban residence among non‐migrants, and the direction of movement among migrants. Two findings emerge. First, mobility in Laos is multidirectional rather than a single rural‐to‐urban flow: measured against rural–urban migration, rural–rural movement is about three times as common, and urban–urban and urban–rural flows each about twice as common. Second, ownership and renting point in opposite directions: agricultural land and home ownership accompany staying and rural‐bound movement, while renting and internet access accompany urban‐oriented mobility. Notably, urban residence does not preclude landholding: most urban residents still own farmland. These findings extend the population geography of assets and mobility beyond the rural‐to‐urban paradigm, revealing a household‐level dual attachment in which the same assets anchor and enable mobility at once.

articles.title: Why Comply? Explaining Sectoral Patterns in GRECO 'S Anti‐Corruption Recommendations
articles.abstract: Why do states vary in their compliance with international anti‐corruption recommendations? Research often treats the state as a unitary actor and explains variation at country‐level. This article challenges that assumption by examining variation in compliance across institutional sectors within countries. Using original data from the Council of Europe's Group of States against Corruption (GRECO), the analysis shows a clear sectoral pattern. Recommendations addressed to prosecutors are implemented most frequently, followed by those targeting judges, while recommendations directed at members of parliament show the lowest levels of compliance. The article explains this variation through the political economy of target compliance. Reform outcomes depend on the interaction between the political costs imposed by reform and the degree of control that targeted actors exercise over its implementation. We find little evidence that country‐level factors shape reform outcomes, while sector‐specific incentives provide a stronger explanation for compliance patterns. By highlighting the importance of the target population, the article contributes to research on international compliance, anti‐corruption governance, and international monitoring mechanisms.

articles.title: A Rapid Systematic Map of Youth Engagement With Marine Environments in a Changing Climate
articles.authors: Carlo Ceglia, Alexandra C. Morel, Lorraine van Blerk
articles.abstract: This paper offers a rapid systematic map of existing qualitative literature on the relationship(s) between marine environments and youth in a changing climate. Building upon recent public, scientific, and scholarly trends that draw attention to the value the ocean holds for both socio‐economic prosperity and climate regulation, this systematic map asks: What evidence emerges from qualitative studies of youth engagement with marine environments in a changing climate? The mapping identified 20 articles thematically coded under three categories—namely, (i) youth experiences of marine environments and climate change, (ii) marine‐based pedagogical approaches to climate change, and (iii) creative strategies and new media. Along with these 3 main categories, the mapping identified different cross‐cutting themes that the 20 studies share. These were discussed as (a) the importance of intergenerational dynamics and intergenerational justice, (b) the lack of youth's insights in marine‐based climate discourses, and (c) the need for place‐based socio‐cultural and economic interventions. After presenting and discussing the results, this rapid systematic map concludes by indicating areas for further research. Specifically, it highlights the need for more place‐based, granular approaches that engage young people on their own terms and experiences as having tremendous value for articulating more ocean‐ and climate‐sensitive interventions. At the same time, it cautions that those same interventions must feed into wider socio‐economic and institutional dynamics that account for the historical responsibilities of a changing climate.

articles.title: How Recipients Compose Their News Sources Online: Utilizing Tracking Data to Investigate Digital News Media Repertoires
articles.authors: Robin Leuppert, Jule Scheper, Nico Spreen, Elena Link
articles.abstract: Today’s high-choice media environment offers various opportunities for interest-driven news exposure, resulting in highly diverse and fragmented news usage patterns, especially in the digital media environment. Media repertoires provide a suitable theoretical framework for considering these circumstances and investigating the entirety and interrelatedness of individuals’ news sources, rather than focusing on singular news offerings. We explore media repertoires focusing on news by relying on behavioral tracking data from 805 German respondents over eleven weeks (November 2022–January 2023). Conducting a latent class analysis based on news usage frequencies across seventeen news categories, we identified eight digital news media repertoires with distinct usage patterns. Repertoire comparisons via analysis of variance (ANOVA) further revealed differences in the news topics used, users’ diversity of news outlets, news concentration, and news usage duration. Implications for future research on investigating media repertoire compositions are discussed.

articles.title: The Policy Umwelt: How AI Problem Representations Render Governance Alternatives Unthinkable
articles.abstract: This paper investigates how AI narratives actively constrain the horizon of conceivable governance options. Moving beyond the established finding that narratives influence policy, we argue they fundamentally prefigure the scope of the politically thinkable by creating what we term “Policy Umwelten.” Adapting Jakob von Uexküll’s concept, a Policy Umwelt describes the perceptible and actionable landscape of interventions available within a given narrative, which systematically renders alternatives invisible. We analyze three competing narratives: Existential Risk, Accelerationism, and Critical AI. We do so through a “What’s the Problem Represented to Be?” analysis of their foundational manifestos. Each constructs a distinct Umwelt: Existential Risk makes global technocratic containment imperative; Accelerationism legitimizes only deregulation and market liberation; and Critical AI centers structural reform. Despite their overt conflict, these narratives converge in constructing Policy Umwelten that render a pragmatic approach to governance difficult to perceive: one that emphasizes iterative learning from empirical feedback and institutional flexibility over grand visions or predetermined certainties. The paper concludes that the most significant constraint on AI policy is not a lack of options but a collective failure of political perception. The Policy Umwelt concept thus provides a diagnostic tool for mapping ideological deadlock and identifying pathways toward more adaptive and less deterministic technological futures.

articles.title: Whose Digital Future? Civil Society and Alternative Imaginaries in Transnational Digital Governance
articles.abstract: This article investigates different visions of digital futures, examining how desired futures are discursively constructed within civil society in transnational digital governance. The analysis builds on discourse theory and a growing body of research on imaginaries in digital governance. Through a discourse‐theoretical analysis of submission papers to the United Nations' Global Digital Compact, the article examines how different collective actors within civil society construct and mobilise desired futures in the institutional context of the UN. The study finds discursive elements that articulate three distinct digital futures: technological progress, societal balance and transformative change. While their objectives, obstacles and enablers are constructed in diverse ways, in all three, digital technologies are considered necessary. By illuminating different normative values and the affective potential through which individuals and collectives are positioned in relation to desired futures, these findings show a variety of articulations within civil society and offer insights into its normative and political roles. In doing so, this study contributes to an understanding of the possibilities and limitations of alternatives in digital governance.

articles.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on heat thresholds for maternal health and birth outcomes
articles.authors: Clara S. Heil, Leonidas G. Ioannou, Günter Alce, Susanne Frennert, Chuansi Gao
articles.abstract: Global warming poses major public health challenges, with pregnant individuals particularly vulnerable to heat. We aim to synthesise evidence on the effects of ambient heat on pregnancy and birth outcomes and identify heat thresholds associated with increased risk of these adverse outcomes. We searched Medline, Web of Science, Scopus, GreenFile and Cinahl (June 2024) for peer-reviewed studies reporting thresholds for ambient heat; heat from medical devices, saunas, pools or studies on conception, IVF, postnatal health were excluded. Participants within studies are limited to individuals capable of becoming pregnant, including women and those identifying differently. Risk of bias is assessed using the Office of Health Assessment and Translation tool. Findings are narratively synthesised according to outcome and exposure metric, and a random effects meta-regression is used to estimate heat thresholds for acute heat effects on adverse outcomes. Evidence is limited by heterogeneity and methodological variability among studies included, and through review process limitations, including no independent dual data extraction and single person performing quality assessment. Meta-analyses determine Tmax thresholds 30.55 °C, 34.11 °C and 39.07 °C for 5%, 10% and 20% risk increase (21 studies, sample=5,589,862), suggesting increasing risk of adverse pregnancy and birth outcomes with increasing heat. The narrative syntheses (103 studies, sample=41,951,950) identifies heterogeneous indicators and a lack of comprehensive heat stress indices. Funding was received through the European Union’s Horizon Framework Programme and UKRI Innovate. PROSPERO registration: CRD42024610438.

articles.title: Tracking funding disparities in global health aid with machine learning
articles.authors: Finn Stürenburg, Kerstin Forster, Nicolas Banholzer, Malte Toetzke, Kenneth Harttgen, Stefan Feuerriegel
articles.abstract: Reducing the global burden of disease is crucial for improving health outcomes. However, misalignment between health aid and country-level disease burden leaves vulnerable populations without the necessary support for major health challenges, particularly in the least developed countries. Here, we develop a machine learning pipeline using large language models to track flows in official development assistance (ODA) earmarked for health and identify aid–burden misalignment. We classified 3.7 million development aid projects from 2000 to 2022 (USD ~ 332 billion) into 17 major categories of communicable, maternal, neonatal, and nutritional diseases (CMNNDs) and non-communicable diseases (NCDs). We compared the rank of per capita ODA disbursement against the rank of disease burden, measured in disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). We interpret DALY-based alignment as a policy-relevant heuristic rather than a prescriptive allocation criterion. Although funding and disease burden are significantly correlated for many diseases, there are notable disparities. For example, NCDs account for 59.5% of global DALYs but received only 2.5% of health-related ODA over the study period. This is concerning because low- and middle-income countries face an increasing double burden from both CMNNDs and NCDs. Our results show aid–burden misalignment across multiple diseases in several regions, including Central Africa and parts of South Asia and West Africa. Overall, our results identify health disparities to potentially inform policy decisions on development assistance and support targeted allocation of health aid.

articles.title: The Tangrams Codeswitching Corpus
articles.authors: Anne L. Beatty-Martínez, Jiaze Li, Yumeng Shen, Stanislav Mulík, Robert D. Hawkins, Rosa E. Guzzardo Tamargo, Paola E. Dussias
articles.abstract: Most research in the language sciences has centered on monolingual data, limiting the relevance of its insights for multilingual populations. The Tangrams Codeswitching Corpus , a Spanish-English dataset containing 30,858 words from 45 dyadic repeated reference games, bridges this gap by offering a richly annotated dataset on bilingual communication and codeswitching. In addition to the corpus, the dataset includes detailed metadata on language experience and proficiency of 90 habitual codeswitchers, enabling studies of individual differences in social coordination and switching behavior. This publicly available resource is valuable for exploring bilinguals’ language choices and the interactional dynamics through which they communicate, collaborate, and coordinate with one another. By providing a transdisciplinary perspective on codeswitching, this dataset offers a unique opportunity to explore how bilinguals adapt their language choices and communicative behavior in everyday interaction.

articles.title: From Fringe to Power in the TikTok Age: Libertarian Ideology and Transgressive Performances in Milei’s ‘Populism Without the People’
articles.authors: Ana Ines Langer, Lluis de Nadal, Eugenia Mitchelstein
articles.abstract: Democracies around the world are under strain from radical right populist leaders and parties, raising urgent questions about their appeal. One way to approach this is by examining what and how they communicate on social media. TikTok warrants close attention, not only as the fastest-growing platform for news and information, but also because of the wider ‘Tiktokification’ of social media and the growing importance of visual communication. Yet populist communication on TikTok has received little attention, reflecting a broader text-centric bias in the literature. Here, we trace Javier Milei’s journey from the political margins to the Argentine presidency through his communication on TikTok, a platform considered key to his electoral success. We combine content analysis of text, visual and performative dimensions and show that Milei rarely appeals to ‘the people’—striking given ‘people-centrism’ is typically considered populism’s defining feature. This is, however, consistent with his right-wing libertarian ideology, which elevates individual freedom over collective solidarity, and is fitting with TikTok’s individualised mode of consumption. Milei’s populism without ‘the people,’ as we call it, combines contempt for the State, anti-elitism and transgressive performances that, as our regression analysis reveals, generate higher engagement. These findings advance our understanding of populism beyond the Global North and for a leader celebrated by the populist radical right worldwide, with broader implications for the relationship between populism, digital media and liberal democracy.

Who belongs to the demos? Undemocratic penalties to immigrant minority representation
articles.authors: Beyza E. Buyuker, Alexandra Filindra, Mia K. Gandenberger, Eva T. Green, Anita Manatschal
articles.abstract: Opposition to political candidates who represent ethnic minority interests in Western societies has included calls for undemocratic penalties. Majority groups in democratic societies value democracy in principle, but such support is malleable. We argue that diverse societies lack consensus on who constitutes the “demos”, the imagined political community. When there is a mismatch between a citizen’s understanding of the demos and an officeholder’s background and/or agenda, citizens may be open to imposing undemocratic penalties by reclassifying the offender as a demos-outsider and/or the punishing action as democratic. We tested our expectations with three survey experiments in the US and Switzerland that varied the candidate’s background (majority v. immigrant minority) and agenda (advocating for an age quota v. ethnic diversity quota). Results confirm that citizens do not behave as principled democrats but rather use their understanding of the demos to support or reject undemocratic penalties against minority politicians and policies. Their vision of the demos also determines whether they perceive the candidate as a demos-outsider (not “true” American/Swiss) and his banning as democratic. Interestingly, support for undemocratic penalties is on average higher in Switzerland than in the US, and slight nuances in the empirical results point to certain contextual contingencies of our results. Overall, our cross-country results suggest that people’s understanding of democracy is not based on firm institutional and procedural criteria, but on distinct visions about who belongs, and who does not.

articles.title: Uneven patterns of cross-border media coverage following natural disasters
articles.abstract: Many natural disasters central to climate-policy debates are hydro-meteorological hazards, yet it remains unclear how media attention is distributed across disaster types. Using 135 million news articles from 466 sources in 123 countries since 2016, we estimated cross-border reporting changes after disasters. Attention rises but is highly uneven (95% confidence intervals are shown in parentheses after the estimates): short-run increases are largest following earthquakes ( β = 0.0785 (0.0758, 0.0812)), dry-mass movements ( β = 0.0531 (0.0349, 0.0713)) and volcanic eruptions ( β = 0.0425 (0.0359, 0.0490)), and smaller for floods ( β = 0.0069 (0.0062, 0.0076)) and droughts ( β = 0.0001 (−0.0036, 0.0039)). Conditional on severity and duration, hydro-meteorological disasters receive less attention than geophysical disasters ( θ = −0.0065 (−0.0115, −0.0015)). Coverage is higher for 100+ versus 0–9 deaths ( β = 0.0360 (0.0231, 0.0490)), with stronger fatality gradients for country pairs with tighter social ties ( β = 0.1498 (0.0822, 0.2174)) and ancestral relatedness ( β = 0.2965 (0.1887, 0.4043)).

articles.title: Diversity of circular economies from Global South evidence
articles.authors: Lucas Straub, Philipp Trotter, Elsie Onsongo, Detlef van Vuuren, Julian Kirchherr
articles.abstract: The circular economy (CE) is widely viewed as a key global lever for sustainable resource use. However, CE conceptualizations have focused mostly on high resource use in the Global North, largely neglecting the drivers, solutions and enablers of circularity in the socio-economic contexts of the Global South. Here, based on a systematic review of 183 peer-reviewed articles, we assess how CE manifests in the Global South. We find circular solutions to be considerably more bottom-up, centring around community-level and often informal practices rather than the top-down, policy and industrially driven activities that dominate the Global North-informed CE literature. CE motivations similarly differ, being primarily rooted in socio-economic needs and cultural practices rather than environmental concerns. Finally, CE enablers are often based on socially and technically adaptive approaches rather than technological innovation. These differences reveal that inclusive circular pathways for sustainable development depend strongly on context, suggesting the need for more flexible and empirically grounded CE concepts.

articles.title: Population dispersion around cities as a driver of global urban land expansion
articles.authors: Francesco Orsi, Diego Valbuena, Alvaro Hopkins
articles.abstract: Urbanization implies a massive expansion of built-up land globally. The magnitude of this phenomenon, however, largely depends on the degree to which growing urban populations spatially concentrate around existing settlements. Here we measure population centrality, or the inverse of residents’ average travel time to the urban core, in over 7000 urban areas worldwide between 2000 and 2020, and test its association with urban land expansion. We observe rising dispersion (i.e., lower centrality) in most urban areas everywhere except Europe and the Americas. This is concerning as the two variables are negatively related: all else being equal, each additional minute from the urban core comes with an extra 1.6 km 2 of built-up land. The association, however, is clearly negative only in small- to mid-sized and low- to mid-income urban areas, but poorly so otherwise. Moreover, higher centrality goes hand-in-hand with a modest containment of built-up land in Southeast Asia, Europe, Canada, and the USA, and an expansion of it in Eastern Asia and Oceania. Our findings suggest that increasing centrality may be a powerful tool for curbing urban land expansion in certain contexts, but an ineffective one in others, and that planning is needed to mitigate the spillovers of centralization.

articles.title: Nature-based solutions for whom - Europeanization and co-optation of collaborative NBS in authoritarian Belgrade
articles.abstract: This paper explores how Nature-Based Solutions (NBS), introduced through processes of Europeanization, are grounded in, and co-opted by, the post-socialist, neoliberal, and increasingly authoritarian Belgrade. The analysis focuses on the EU-funded CLEVER Cities project, which introduced NBS to Belgrade through the Linear Park, which was later absorbed into Marina Dorćol—a commercial waterfront development by European investors. Despite being celebrated as a best - practice example, the paper indicates that the NBS framework built on participation and socio-ecological benefits is turned into a tool for profit-making and political legitimation by an increasingly authoritarian Serbian regime. Building on document and media analysis, the paper identifies how this local co-optation of NBS is both mediated and reinforced by processes of Europeanization. The findings contribute to the critical debates on NBS by revealing structural limitations rooted not only in the local context but also in the way NBS are created and diffused in Europe. The paper argues for more politically reflexive approaches to NBS that prioritize power redistribution and social justice across diverse urban contexts.
